issues.text: For a real number p∈(1,∞) and a positive integer n, equip ℝn with the distance dp(x,y)=(Σj=1n|xj-yj|p)1/p. A finite subset S⊂ℝn is equilateral if there exists a real number r>0 such that dp(x,y)=r for every two distinct points x,y∈ S. Determine exactly the set of exponents p∈(1,∞) for which, for every positive integer n, every equilateral subset of (ℝn,dp) has at most n+1 elements. Give the parameter set in interval notation.

For each positive integer n, let a(n) be the least nonnegative integer m for which there exist integers x0,…,xm with x0=1, xm=n, and the following property: for every k=1,…,m, there are indices 0≤ i,j<k such that xk equals one of xi+xj, xi-xj, or xi xj. The indices i,j may be equal, earlier values may be reused, and intermediate values have no sign or magnitude restrictions. Determine the increasing ordered tuple of all primes p<5000 satisfying a(p)<a(p-1).

For a positive integer s, consider the following iteration in exact real arithmetic. Let n≥1, let A∈ℝn× n satisfy AT=A and vT Av>0 for every nonzero v∈ℝn, and choose b,x0∈ℝn. Define x*=A-1b, rk=b-Axk, ‖v‖A=(vT Av)1/2. If rk=0, terminate. Otherwise, set Ks(A,rk)=span{rk,Ark,…,As-1rk} and let xk+1 be the unique minimizer of ‖x*-z‖A over z∈ xk+Ks(A,rk). Each such minimization is one restart block, so k counts blocks. For a nonterminating orbit, define yk=(rk)/(‖rk‖2), ‖v‖2=(vT v)1/2. Determine the smallest positive integer s for which there exist n,A,b,x0 as above such that rk≠0 for every k≥0, but (y2k)k≥0 does not converge in Euclidean norm. Return +∞ if no such integer exists.

Let I={4,6,8,…}∪{∞}. For each finite m∈ I, set Rm=√((2π)/(m sin(2π/m))), and let Pm⊂ℝ2 be the interior of the convex hull of the points Rm( cos((2k+1)π/m), sin((2k+1)π/m)), k=0,…,m-1. Set P∞={x∈ℝ2:‖x‖2<1}. Thus every member of this family is a centrally symmetric convex domain of area π. For any domain Ω in this family, define FΩ(ξ)=∫Ω eiξ· x dx, κ(Ω)=inf{‖ξ‖2:ξ∈ℝ2, FΩ(ξ)=0}, where dx is planar Lebesgue measure, the inner product and norm are Euclidean, and inf∅=+∞. Determine the unique maximizing index m*∈ I satisfying κ(Pm_*)=supm∈ Iκ(Pm).

Work in the Euclidean plane with the lattice ℤ2 of points having integer coordinates. All circles may have arbitrary real centers and positive radii. For a nonnegative integer n, an n-circle is a circle whose open interior contains exactly n lattice points; lattice points on its circumference are not counted. An n-circle is called largest if its radius is at least the radius of every other n-circle. Call n strong if a largest n-circle exists but no largest (n+1)-circle exists. For a circle C, let D(C)=C∩ℤ2 be its set of boundary lattice points. Say that D(C) has a mirror symmetry if reflection across some affine line in the plane maps D(C) onto itself. Determine the smallest strong integer n for which there exists a largest n-circle C such that D(C) has no mirror symmetry.

For complex q with |q|<1, define P(q)=∏m=0∞((1-q8m+1)(1-q8m+7))/((1-q8m+3)(1-q8m+5)). For each real δ, define the coefficients cδ(n) by exp(δ log P(q))=Σn=0∞cδ(n)qn, where log P(q) is the holomorphic logarithm on the open unit disk normalized by log P(0)=0. Set (σ0,σ1,σ2,σ3,σ4,σ5,σ6,σ7)=(1,-1,1,1,-1,1,-1,-1). Determine, as an exact interval, the set of all exponents δ∈(2,4] for which σr cδ(8m+r)≥ 0 for every integer m≥0 and every r∈{0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7}. Zero coefficients are allowed.

Let X=(xij)i,j=13 and Y=(yij)i,j=13 have eighteen algebraically independent commuting indeterminates over ℝ as entries. For a 3×3 matrix A=(aij), define its permanent by per(A)=Σσ∈ S_3∏i=13ai,σ(i), where S3 is the set of all permutations of {1,2,3}, and let det(A) denote the usual determinant. For a sign matrix S=(sij)∈{-1,1}3×3, define the entrywise product S∘ A=(sijaij). Determine the smallest positive integer k for which there exist sign matrices S1,…,Sk,T1,…,Tk∈{-1,1}3×3 and real constants c1,…,ck, independent of all eighteen indeterminates, such that the polynomial identity per(X)per(Y)=Σt=1kctdet(St∘ X)det(Tt∘ Y) holds.

All graphs are finite, simple, and undirected. Cycles are considered as subgraphs, not necessarily induced subgraphs. A graph homomorphism from G to H is a map f:V(G)→ V(H) such that f(u)f(v)∈ E(H) whenever uv∈ E(G); the map need not be injective. For a real number c∈[0,1], consider the following property: there exists a finite graph Hc containing no cycle of length 3 such that, for every integer n≥1, every graph G on n vertices containing no cycle of length 3 or 5, and in which every vertex has at least cn neighbors, admits a homomorphism to Hc. The graph Hc may depend on c, but not on n or G. What is the exact infimum of the numbers c∈[0,1] having this property?

For each integer k∈{1,2,…,14}, set L=8k+3 and h=4k+2, and index length-L sequences by 0,1,…,L-1. Define q∈{-1,1}L by setting qi=-1 exactly at the three indices h-1,h,L-1, and qi=1 elsewhere. For any x∈{-1,1}L, define its half-flip x* by xi*=xi for i<h and xi*=-xi for i≥ h. Multiplication of sequences is coordinatewise, so (sq)i=siqi. For 1≤ d<L, define the aperiodic autocorrelation Cd(x)=Σi=0L-1-dxi xi+d, with no wrap-around of indices. Determine the finite set of all such integers k for which there exists s∈{-1,1}L satisfying Cd(s)+Cd(s*)+Cd(sq)+Cd((sq)*)=0 for every d=1,2,…,L-1.

All graphs in this question are finite, nonempty, simple, and undirected. A graph is planar if it admits a drawing in the plane in which edges meet only at common endpoints. Let B be the class of graphs G=(V,E) satisfying both conditions: 1. There exist planar graphs P1=(V,E1) and P2=(V,E2) such that E=E1∪ E2. The edge sets may overlap, and the two planar drawings are chosen independently. 2. No three distinct vertices of G are pairwise nonadjacent. For a graph G, define its chromatic number χ(G) to be the least positive integer k for which there is a map c:V→{1,…,k} satisfying c(u)≠ c(v) for every edge uv∈ E. Determine the exact value of maxG∈Bχ(G).

Work in the Euclidean plane ℝ2 with its standard metric. Set δ=1/500000, u(x,y)=(480x+31y)/(481), v(x,y)=(-31x+480y)/(481). Consider the three conics Q0: x2-(25/3)xy+(600/29)y2-(15/2)x-(2975/29)y+25/2=0; Q1: y2-δ2(x+3/4)2+δ4=0; Q2: v(x,y)2-δ2(u(x,y)-297/323)2+δ4=0. A real circle means a locus Ca,b,r: (x-a)2+(y-b)2=r2, a,b∈ℝ, r>0. Tangency to a conic means that the circle and the conic share a point in ℝ2 at which their tangent lines coincide. Count each distinct circle once, without orientation or algebraic multiplicity and regardless of the choice of contact points. What is the exact number of real circles simultaneously tangent to Q0,Q1,Q2?
